title: Project Blue Book and the Pentagon report contradict each other

As a result of these investigations and studies and experience gained from investigating UFO reports since 1948, the conclusions of Project BLUE BOOK are:(1) no UFO reported, investigated, and evaluated by the Air Force has ever given any indication of threat to our national security;(2) there has been no evidence submitted to or discovered by the Air Force that sightings categorized as "unidentified" represent technological developments or principles beyond the range of present-day scientific knowledge, and (3) there has been no evidence indicating that sightings categorized as "unidentified" are extraterrestrial vehicles.

plain: The government's old word on UFOs and its newer word do not fit together, so one of them must be wrong. That is the argument of the researcher Eric Weinstein, who puts it to Michels in 2022 during a debate on the show. On one side is Project Blue Book, the US Air Force's UFO study of the 1950s and 60s; on the other is the Pentagon's 2021 report to Congress on UAP, the government's newer term for UFOs, meaning unidentified aerial phenomena. Weinstein says that "either we were lying then that there's nothing to see" and "telling the truth now," and if so, the earlier official story was not straight with the public. An Air Force fact sheet of January 1985 sets out Blue Book's conclusions: that no UFO it investigated "has ever given any indication of threat to our national security," that there was no evidence the "unidentified" sightings showed technology "beyond the range of present-day scientific knowledge," and no evidence they "are extraterrestrial vehicles." The fact sheet speaks of what was submitted to or found by the Air Force; whether that sits at odds with the later Pentagon report is Weinstein's reading, and the fact sheet itself does not compare the two.
